corrections.claimed_speedup: README makes no speed claim. Suite data for the mogwai 0.6.5 keyed entry (derived from page data): geometric mean over the 9 CPU benchmarks of the median total duration (medians computed from the raw run arrays in results.ts) is 0.719x the time of React 19.2 hooks (about 1.39x faster) and 1.310x the time of vanillajs-keyed. The non-keyed mogwai 0.6.5 entry is 1.313x the time of vanillajs-non-keyed (0.679x keyed React, a cross-mode comparison). Medians for the keyed entry: create 1,000 rows 23.9 ms vs React 23.6 ms and vanilla 20.6 ms; swap 1,000 rows 13.0 ms vs React 89.7 ms; create 10,000 rows 357.4 ms vs React 401.0 ms; append rows 37.8 ms vs React 29.3 ms.
corrections.caveats: Independent public suite measured on a MacBook Pro 14 M4 with Chrome 154.0.8037.98 (App.tsx), but the page labels the run a development snapshot and the prebuilt bundle's Rust toolchain is not recorded, so tier B not A (same rules as Leptos and Sycamore). The measured build is mogwai 0.6.5 (crates.io 2023-02-01) with the mogwai-js-framework-benchmark 0.1.0 app crate (2023-02-02) and mogwai-dom 0.2.x (last release 0.2.6, 2023-10-29); the current crate is 0.8.0 (2026-09-26) and its API (View trait, rsx! macro, events as futures) differs, so the suite numbers describe the old version, not current mogwai. The suite attaches note #1139 (implementation does not pass the strict CSP check). Slower than vanilla JavaScript on all 9 CPU benchmarks (1.31x geometric-mean time, derived), slower than React on append rows (1.29x React's time) and create 1,000 rows (1.01x), and worse than React on first paint (306.3 vs 226.6 ms), memory (run memory 9.65 vs 4.37 MB) and compressed size (66.3 vs 51.4 kB). The geometric-mean win over React is dominated by swap rows (13.0 ms vs 89.7 ms). Against the per-benchmark best keyed entry it is 1.37x behind (derived; the earlier 1.59x figure mixed in non-keyed entries). Ratios are unweighted geometric means from results.ts, not the site's weighted score. No LICENSE or COPYING file exists at the repository root; the MIT licence comes from crates.io metadata (every listed version declares MIT). The bundle is checked in prebuilt (build-prod is a no-op).

notes: Numbers recompute exactly from results.ts (0.719x React, 1.310x vanilla keyed). tier_reason: performance.md times parasail against SSW, Opal, SWIPE and ssearch36 with exact command lines (harness apps/parasail_aligner.cpp in the repo), compiler Intel ICC 15.0.1 -O3 and CPU Xeon E5-2670 v3 for the Haswell table, so A; all quoted numbers are on the page.

corrections.claimed_speedup: performance.md, Intel Haswell E5-2670 v3 table (seconds per database search for the 110/195/390/513-residue queries, mean of three runs): SSW (SSE2) 12.0 / 25.6 / 41.5 / 48.7; parasail AVX2 16-bit 9.3 / 12.0 / 17.4 / 21.5 (about 1.3x, 2.1x, 2.4x and 2.3x faster than SSW, derived from page data); parasail SSE4.1 16-bit 10.8 / 15.9 / 27.4 / 33.8 (about 1.1x to 1.6x, derived from page data). MacBook Pro i5 table: SSW (SSE2) 13.2 / 27.1 / 41.7 / 52.4 vs parasail SSE4.1 16-bit 11.3 / 15.9 / 25.8 / 36.9 (about 1.2x to 1.7x, derived from page data). SWIPE (SSSE3) is faster than parasail SSE4.1 16-bit on all four queries on the MacBook (7.6 / 13.3 / 24.7 / 32.0 s) but on Haswell only at 110 residues (9.6 vs 10.8 s); there parasail SSE4.1 16-bit is faster at 195, 390 and 513 residues and parasail AVX2 16-bit beats SWIPE, Opal AVX2 and ssearch36 on all four queries.
corrections.caveats: The win is against SSW only in the narrow sense of a 2015-era SSE2 kernel: AVX2 rows compare different instruction sets than SSW's SSE2, and the page names one compiler and -O3 for the Haswell runs without saying how each competitor was built. The numbers were committed in June-July 2015 (performance.md history ends 2015-07-11) against a pre-1.0 parasail whose commit is not pinned. SWIPE (a database-search specialist) is faster than parasail SSE4.1 on every MacBook query and at 110 residues on Haswell, and parasail's 8-bit 'sat' SSE4.1 variant is slower than SSW at the longer queries on Haswell (44.4 vs 41.5 s at 390 and 55.2 vs 48.7 s at 513 residues). Only scores are computed, not alignments or tracebacks. The Swiss-Prot release is not stated. No SeqAn or scalar Smith-Waterman row appears on the page. The BMC Bioinformatics 2016 paper was not opened (NCBI blocked); a search-result summary only says SWIPE is 1.2 to 2.4 times faster than parasail for sequences under 500 residues and parasail is faster for longer ones (snippet, not verified; this disagrees with the Haswell SSE4.1 16-bit rows). The license (LICENSE.md, Battelle Memorial Institute) is BSD-3-Clause-like text plus a clause that redistributions and publications 'should include' a citation of the 2016 BMC paper; it is not an SPDX-listed or OSI-approved license, so usability is reference. Last commit seen on the master branch (2025-08-27); the develop branch was not checked.

notes: All quoted numbers are on performance.md; the claim that SWIPE beats parasail SSE4.1 on both machines was wrong for Haswell (SWIPE wins only at 110 residues) and is corrected. Usability changed to reference because the Battelle licence is not OSI-approved (BSD-3-like plus a soft citation clause; orchestrator may judge it copyable). Shortcomings: 2015 numbers on unpinned pre-1.0 code, AVX2 vs SSE2 instruction-set asymmetry, SWIPE faster on the MacBook, score-only workload.
